summary: Presents a framework for supporting authorized emergency communications in IP telephony, in line with the Emergency Telecommunications Service. It sets objectives for how this should work within the existing internet architecture. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4190 sets out how emergency calls should be handled when they travel over IP networks. It says the network has to be able to recognise an authorised emergency call, give it priority over ordinary traffic, and stop it being dropped or forged. It describes how existing protocols could carry that information instead of defining a new one.

questions: how to prioritize emergency voip calls
subtitle: What the network would need to know and do to give authorised emergency calls a better chance of getting through.

tldr.problem: Emergency calls over IP telephony compete with ordinary traffic on a network whose default service model is best effort, so they can be blocked exactly when they are needed.
tldr.mechanism: The document sets out objectives for emergency traffic and maps them onto existing protocols: SIP for setting the call up, Diff-Serv code points for marking packets, and policy, traffic engineering, security and routing mechanisms to protect the marked traffic.
tldr.outcome: It defines no protocol of its own. It is an Informational framework that says emergency support will never be available everywhere, and that it must work even where only some networks along the path support it.

today: RFC 4190 is an Informational document from November 2005 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines no protocol of its own: it is a framework of objectives that maps them onto existing IETF protocols, together with two worked scenarios and a discussion of parallel work in other standards bodies.

sections.title: Why Emergency Calls Over IP Need Their Own Rules
sections.content:
Emergency calls already exist in the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN). Services such as 911 in the United States and 999 in the United Kingdom are available to the general public. Other emergency telephone services involve authorised users only, and they are the subject of this document.

The Internet offers no equivalent. Its default service model is best effort, which means the network forwards each packet as best it can and reserves no resources for it, so an emergency call over IP telephony competes with ordinary traffic and can be blocked when the network is congested. Interactive voice tolerates a lower combination of loss, delay and jitter than applications such as email, which places a heavier burden on the problem. Toll-quality service assumes better than best effort, which raises the chance of call blocking further.

The document therefore aims at something modest: it does not try to copy the exact capabilities of existing PSTN emergency voice service, because the two architectures differ too much for that. It gives network operators and telephony carriers a common set of objectives, and a way to constrain customer expectations about what emergency service over IP can deliver.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet treats every packet the same way, so an emergency call can be delayed like any other call when the network is busy. RFC 4190 describes what the network would need to know and do to give authorised emergency calls a better chance of getting through.

sections.title: The Emergency Services That Exist Today
sections.content:
Two existing services set the model. The Government Emergency Telecommunications Service (GETS) is a United States service overseen by the National Communications System, and unlike 911 it is accessible only to authorised individuals. Most of those are staff of government agencies such as the Department of Transportation, NASA, the Department of Defense and the Federal Emergency Management Agency, plus a selected set of people in private industry, including telecommunications companies and utilities, who take part in critical infrastructure recovery. The purpose of GETS is to achieve a high probability that phone service will be available to those people during emergencies such as hurricanes and earthquakes, when the general public may be blocking calls on the telephone network. GETS is based in part on the ANSI T1.631 standard, which specifies a High Probability of Completion for SS7 signalling.

The International Emergency Preparedness Scheme (IEPS) is an ITU standard describing emergency-related communications over the international telephone service. Where systems like GETS are national in scope, IEPS extends local or national authorised emergency call establishment and provides a building block for a global service. Like GETS, it promotes extended queuing, alternate routing and exemption from restrictive management controls, to increase the probability that international emergency calls will be established. The specifics are left to later ITU documents.
sections.plainLanguage: Two existing services shape the design. GETS in the United States gives authorised government and utility staff a better chance of getting a call through during a disaster. The ITU's IEPS standard extends the same idea to international calls.

sections.title: Five Areas Where Support Has to Come From
sections.content:
The framework divides what is needed into five areas: signaling, policy, traffic engineering, security and routing. The document is explicit that these are separate measures with no dependency on each other as a whole, and that not all of them are needed in every case. Emergency support is not expected to be a service that is available everywhere.

One constraint shapes the whole design. Inter-domain emergency communication should not rely on widespread support along the path between the end points. At the network layer there may be islands of support realised as overlay networks, and a solution may instead be constrained on an end-to-end basis at the transport or application layer. Designers and deployers have to take that diversity and partial support into account.

The document also notes that other standards bodies already have architectures and protocols for emergency communication, and that interoperating with them through gateways would create a need to distinguish emergency flows from other flows, for example so that emergency service can be triggered from an IP network. The discussion of protocols in the next section is written so that it does not violate the requirements of the general and IP telephony ETS requirement documents, without mapping each protocol to a requirement one for one.
sections.plainLanguage: The document splits the work into five parts: how calls are set up and marked, what rules apply, how the network is tuned, how calls are protected, and how traffic finds a route. Each part can be used on its own, and a network may support only some of them.

sections.title: Marking a Call as an Emergency Call
sections.content:
Signaling conveys information to intermediate or end nodes. It can travel out of band, in a flow of its own such as SIP messages, or in band, as state information inside the datagram carrying the voice data. The second case could be realised as Diff-Serv code points in the IP packet.

SIP already has a priority field in its Request-Header-Field with five defined values: emergency, urgent, normal, non-urgent and other-priority. Those values are meant to convey importance to the end user and carry no additional meaning for the network. Separate requirements for a SIP resource priority header exist, intended to give gateways and proxies an extra distinction they can act on.

For the network to act, a marking has to survive the trip. Diff-Serv markings are not globally unique, and an intermediate node or domain may remove or change them, so the document notes that what is missing is an in-band marking that stays constant end to end. It considers three choices: a new Per-Hop Behaviour dedicated to emergency traffic, a new shim layer protocol above IP, or a new specification in an existing application layer protocol. The first two are architecturally cleanest but are long term efforts, limited by the small number of Diff-Serv code points and by the contention that yet another shim layer creates. Discussions in the Audio/Visual Transport working group centred on a classifier field in an RTP extension header, with values such as authorized-emergency, emergency and normal, but the group expressed a rough consensus not to advance it, citing reliance on SIP to convey importance and the risk of affecting header compression.

In the near term the document suggests using the existing Assured Forwarding behaviour to distinguish emergency traffic, at a minimum for the different SIP call signaling messages. If the domain also supports Expedited Forwarding, that would be used for the IP telephony data packets; otherwise another AF class would be used for those flows.
sections.plainLanguage: SIP already has a priority field with five values, and emergency is one of them. For the network to treat a call specially, the marking has to survive every router on the path, so the document looks at marking the packets themselves and settles on reusing existing Diff-Serv behaviours for now.

sections.title: Finding Another Path When the Network Is Congested
sections.content:
Alternate path routing means discovering and using a different path to route IP telephony traffic around a congestion point. The document makes no assumption about how the alternate path is achieved, or at which layer, but says that even a minimal form of the capability would raise the probability that an emergency call completes by using uncongested paths. It warns that care is needed in how the system provides alternate paths, so that discovery does not itself add enough control traffic to cause the congestion being avoided.

Routing protocols at the IP network layer, such as BGP and OSPF, already contain mechanisms for determining link failure between routing peers, and the discovery automatically propagates information to other routers. In OSPF's Equal Cost Multiple Path the impact of a link failure is minimised because alternate paths to the destination already exist.

Two further areas of IETF work can help with call signaling. The first is a framework for enhancing the LDP specification of MPLS to achieve fault tolerance within a domain; it does not provide alternate path routing itself, but reduces the loss of intradomain connectivity when MPLS is used. The second is Telephony Routing over IP (TRIP), which specifies application level telephony routing regardless of the signalling protocol in use, is modelled after BGP-4, and advertises reachability and attributes of destinations such as LocalPreference and MultiExitDisc. The document rules out extending inter-domain routing for emergency traffic: BGP is already strained by its existing requirements, and features that increase the number of advertised routes would not be well received.
sections.plainLanguage: When part of the network is congested, calls can be sent along a different route instead. The document points to existing routing work, including TRIP for telephony gateways, and deliberately leaves BGP alone.

sections.title: Authorising Emergency Traffic and Protecting It
sections.content:
Any mechanism that raises the priority of a set of flows can be abused to strengthen a denial of service attack. Priority magnifies the effect of attack traffic on bandwidth availability in lower capacity links and increases the likelihood of it reaching its targets, and an attack could tie up resources such as circuits in a PSTN gateway. A provider deploying a priority mechanism must therefore apply access controls and security mechanisms carefully. The priority level for traffic originating from an unauthorised part of a network or ingress point should be reset to normal, and users must be authenticated before being allowed to use a priority service. That authentication should be lightweight, so it does not create opportunities for denial of service attacks against itself, and other security mechanisms should not add so much overhead that they create further opportunities.

Authorisation has to be verified before a flow is given emergency facilities. Where an emergency call is carried from the PSTN to the PSTN over one carrier's IP backbone, little IP-specific authorisation is needed because the user authenticates to the PSTN as usual, for example with a PIN in the United States GETS. The gateway from the PSTN into the backbone must signal that the flow carries an ETS label, and the gateway back into the PSTN must signal the call's label as well. A secure link between the gateways, using IPSec or SIP security functionality, protects the integrity of that signalling against attackers who have reached the backbone network and stops them placing emergency calls through the egress gateway.

Where emergency priority is provided within one domain, that network must use the security features of the priority mechanism it deploys, to ensure the flow came from an authorised user or process. The access network may authorise emergency traffic as part of its own user authentication procedures, at the link, network or higher layers, and it must decide how often to update its list of authorised users based on the traffic it is prepared to accept from recently revoked users. Where emergency traffic moves to inter-domain end-to-end IP, verifying authorisation becomes more complex: the user's access network must verify it before network-layer priority is given, and the administrative domains that agree to exchange emergency traffic must have a means to signal a flow's status to each other securely. The originating network takes responsibility for marking only authorised traffic, but the recipient cannot rely on this happening with complete reliability, so both domains must condition the traffic to prevent theft and denial of service attacks propagating between them.

Communications used to respond to a deliberate attack should be protected end to end with IPSec or the security functionality in SIP and SRTP, so that they cannot be altered or intercepted to worsen the situation, for example by changing the orders to first responders.
sections.plainLanguage: Giving some calls priority also makes it easier to attack the network, so the network has to check who is allowed to use it before it grants it. Emergency calls that cross networks need the label protected in transit, and calls used during an attack should be protected end to end.

viz.caption: THE FIVE AREAS OF SUPPORT THE FRAMEWORK NAMES

items.title: Signaling
items.text: Carrying the fact that a call is an emergency call, either out of band in SIP messages or in band inside the packet.

items.title: Policy
items.text: The rules that decide how much emergency traffic is allowed, and whether existing calls may be preempted.

items.title: Traffic engineering
items.text: Tuning the network so emergency traffic is served, for example with MPLS inside a domain or by overprovisioning the core.

items.title: Security
items.text: Checking that a flow really is authorised before giving it priority, and protecting the signalling that carries the label.

items.title: Routing
items.text: Finding an alternate path when the direct path is congested, without adding traffic that causes more congestion.
